lessons.text: Never use slippery slope (Claiming one step inevitably cascades to catastrophe without support). It cost you against Rumi.
Never use ad hominem (Attacking the arguer instead of the argument). It cost you against Rumi.

Prepare an answer before you assert: Rumi broke through with "But note what just happened: your argument skipped the evidence entirely. Because a four-day week costs more than it returns, the documente…" (Clean argument. structure=0.50, evidence=1.00).

Prepare an answer before you assert: Rumi broke through with "However, your premise assumes what it needs to prove, and the data shows otherwise. When the measured results are compared across studies,…" (Clean argument. structure=1.00, evidence=1.00).

Borrow this pattern from Rumi: "However, your premise assumes what it needs to prove, and the data shows otherwise. When the measured results are compared across studies,…" — it carried evidence, its premises led cleanly to the conclusion.

Your weakest move against Rumi was "Consider the evidence first. When the measured results are compared across studies, then the pattern is consistent, so it follows that a fo…" (soundness 0.20). State its premises and evidence before you use it again.
Never use appeal to emotion (Substituting feeling for reasoning). It cost you against Shing-Tung Yau.

Your winning pattern: "Yet your position leaves the strongest counter-example untouched. The research found the effect repeatedly; since the premise survives test…" — it answered the opponent directly, it carried evidence, its premises led cleanly to the conclusion.
Never use no true scotsman (Redefining a category on the fly to exclude a damaging counterexample). It cost you against Carl Sagan.
